en: The Apadāna of the Elder Buddhupaṭṭhāka Sudhāvagga 10 I was a monk who attended upon the Buddha, Who had attained the supreme enlightenment. I offered him a single *pāyasa* dish; Because of that deed, I have been reborn here. I have lived for eighty-four thousand aeons In the heavenly world, enjoying bliss. From there, passing away from that state, I was reborn in the human world. There too, I enjoyed great happiness; I was a king named Mahāsudassana. My city was Kusāvatī, And it was seven leagues in extent. Seven walls surrounded it, And seven moats were dug around them. It was adorned with seven rows of palm trees, And it was filled with every kind of delight. There, I ruled over the four continents, Possessing the seven treasures and the four bases of power. I was a righteous wheel-turning monarch, A conqueror through righteousness, bringing peace to the world. Having performed such merit in the past, I have now attained this final existence. I am a monk who has reached the end of suffering, One who has crossed over the ocean of birth and death. By attending upon the Teacher, the Buddha, I have realized the fruit of Arhatship. This is my final birth in the world of men; Now, having attained liberation, I am at peace. Thus did the Elder Buddhupaṭṭhāka speak Of his own former deeds in the presence of the Saṅgha. Having heard this, the monks were filled with joy, And they paid homage to the one who had transcended all fear.
“Under the Blessed One Vipassi,
I was a conch-blower; I was ever devoted to standing attendance.”
Behold the fruit of attending upon the Sugata, the Great Seer,
the Tathāgata, the Lord of the World!
Sixty thousand musical instruments always attend upon me;
for ninety-one eons—
I attended upon the great seer;
I do not recognize a state of misery—
this is the fruit of my attendance.
In the twenty-fourth aeon from now,
there were sixteen kings named Mahānigghosa.
Universal monarchs of great power.
The four analytical knowledges... [and so forth]...
“Such is the teaching of the Buddha.
Thus indeed did the Venerable Elder Buddhupaṭṭhāka speak these verses.
This is the tenth legend of the Elder Buddhupaṭṭhāka.
The Tenth Chapter: Sudhāvagga.
Its summary (uddāna) is:
Sudhā, suci, and ceḷa;
Sūcī and Gandhamāliya;
Tipupphiya and Madhusena;
Veyyāvaccaka and Upaṭṭhaka.
Sixty verses in total are recited in this chapter.
Now, the summary of the chapter:
The first chapter is the Buddhavagga;
then the Sīhāsana and Subhūti;
and the Kuṇḍadhāna and Upāli.
And Bījanisākacinti.
Nāgasamāla, Timira,
and Sudhāvagga— these are the ten.
One hundred and fourteen verses,
and fifty-five more:
this is the Ten-Verse Chapter on the Buddhas.
The first hundred stanzas are complete.
